source.title: Towards Atoms of Large Language Models
source.authors: Chenhui Hu; Pengfei Cao; Yubo Chen; Kang Liu; Jun Zhao

record.tranche_reason: The study measures neurons as candidate fundamental representational units and concludes that their low stability makes them unsuitable as ideal atoms. Its stability measure is not a count of semantic jobs per neuron pole, so it does not directly test the listed versions’ specific claims.
record.gate_note: The study reports aggregate faithfulness and stability results for neurons and features. It does not measure pole-level job counts, explanations evaluated on held-out activating examples, or the listed architecture and circuit claims. Other reported results about identified atoms, representation geometry, and monosemanticity do not directly measure the claim’s neuron-pole assertions.
record.test_reason: The study scores neurons with its own structural criteria: faithfulness (R2) and stability (q*), a coherence–sparsity uniqueness statistic. Neither counts how many semantic jobs a neuron or neuron pole has. Its only semantic test (LLM-judge monosemanticity, Fig. 6/45) covers SAE features and TSAE atoms, not neurons. The claim that neurons are polysemantic is an inference from low q*, not a measured rate. So the neuron result is a related construct, not a test of V1–V7.
record.authors_conclusion: The paraphrase is correct. Add that the authors find a representation shift corrected by the atomic inner product. They also find TSAE atoms score more monosemantic than SAE features on an LLM-judge test; neurons were not included in that test.
record.recipe_differences: Uses the authors’ atomic inner product and faithfulness/stability criteria to assess candidate units, rather than auditing neuron-pole interpretations and testing explanations on held-out activations.
record.method_sensitivity: The paper reports that atom identification depends on TSAE capacity matching data scale; the neuron faithfulness and stability values here are reported as aggregates.

fits_no_version.finding: Neurons in Gemma2-2B, Gemma2-9B and Llama3.1-8B have mean stability q* = 0.5% under the AIP coherence–sparsity criterion. The authors read this as implying polysemanticity.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Neuron bases fail a compressed-sensing uniqueness criterion (structural monorepresentationality) for entity representations.

fits_no_version.finding: SAE features reach q* = 68.2% but R2 = 48.8% on entity activations. TSAE atoms reach about 99.9% on both and score higher than features on LLM-judge monosemanticity.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Features trade off stability against faithfulness, while capacity-matched threshold SAEs reach both.

record.peer_reviewed: Proceedings of the 43rd International Conference on Machine Learning, PMLR 306, 2026
record.problems: The neuron results use faithfulness and a structural stability statistic rather than direct semantic job counts; the reported values are averages over layers and models. The paper notes that Llama3.1-8B layers 30 and 31 were omitted from reported results because optimization failed on unusually large activations.
record.rows_left_out: No additional results directly measure neuron-pole job counts or the listed explanation tests. Results on identified atoms, representation shifts, and atom monosemanticity were omitted because they do not measure the listed neuron-pole claims.

untested.parts: No Qwen3-32B audit and no neuron-pole job shares.
No neuron interpretability shares in any model. Gemma2-2B/9B and Llama3.1-8B appear only through structural q*.
No InceptionV1 or vision neurons, and no pose or recursive-generalization analysis.
No test of architecture, regularization or tools as causes of messy neurons.
No attribution graphs built from neurons.
No test of explanations against held-out activations for neurons.
No simulation-based scoring of neuron explanations.

record.verdict_notes: The study is not one of the original sources. Neurons are never scored semantically, so the study cannot speak to job shares despite its statement that neurons are polysemantic. The reader's tranche T5 overstates the relation. The study measures a different construct and gives only a cited/inferred argument about polysemanticity.

versions.untested_parts: The Qwen3-32B audit, positive/negative neuron poles, and proportions with one job, two related jobs, or unexplained jobs are not measured.
The study does not estimate neuron-pole job shares across models or scale; its aggregate neuron stability measure is not such a share.
No InceptionV1 cat-and-car neuron, pose interpretation, or recursive generalization is tested.
The study does not test the proposed architecture/regularization/tool explanation or the InceptionV1-sized vision-model estimates.
No attribution graphs or reconstruction of model behaviour using the model’s own neurons are evaluated.
The study does not test explanations against new activating examples or measure prediction of where a neuron fires.
The study does not score neuron explanations by simulating their activations on new text.

rows.note: The authors interpret low neuron stability as implying polysemanticity. This metric is not a direct semantic job-count measure.
rows.check: q* is a structural uniqueness statistic (µq < 1/(2Kq−1)), not an interpretability or job-count share. The authors' link to polysemanticity is inferred, not measured. The value is averaged over layers and models.
